skill.name: scientific-visualization
skill.description: Create publication-ready scientific figures with matplotlib, seaborn, and plotly using journal sizing, accessible palettes, statistical annotations, and export guidance.
skill.summary: Build journal-ready scientific plots with accessible palettes, panel layouts, and publication export settings.
skill.author: davila7

security_audit.summary: Most static findings are false positives caused by markdown backticks, palette names, reference prose, and dictionary key lookups. One medium filesystem concern is confirmed because scripts/style_presets.py can write a caller-specified style file path. No evidence found of prompt injection, credential access, network calls, or malicious intent.

remediation.issue: Unrestricted output path for style template creation.
remediation.suggestion: Resolve output_file under an intended working directory, reject absolute paths or traversal, or require explicit user confirmation before writing.

remediation.issue: Optional helper script execution is documented inline.
remediation.suggestion: State expected outputs and side effects before suggesting users run helper scripts.

content.value_statement: Scientific figures often fail journal, accessibility, or export requirements. This skill guides figure design, styling, validation, and export for publication workflows.
actual_capabilities: Applies publication style presets for Nature, Science, Cell, PLOS, ACS, and IEEE figure sizing.
Provides colorblind-friendly palettes and colormap guidance for categorical, sequential, and diverging data.
Guides multi-panel layouts, panel labels, error bars, significance markers, and readable typography.
Exports matplotlib figures to PDF, EPS, SVG, PNG, and TIFF with DPI settings.
Checks figure dimensions against journal column widths and height limits.
Offers matplotlib, seaborn, and plotly examples for common scientific chart types.
limitations: Does not verify current journal policies beyond included reference notes.
Does not perform statistical tests or validate scientific conclusions.
Generated figures still require manual review at final print size.
Helper scripts assume Python plotting dependencies are installed locally.

use_cases.title: Prepare Manuscript Figures
use_cases.description: Turn analysis plots into journal-ready figures with correct size, labels, colors, and export formats.

use_cases.title: Standardize Lab Plot Styles
use_cases.description: Create shared plotting defaults so related figures use consistent typography, palettes, and spacing.

use_cases.title: Check Submission Graphics
use_cases.description: Review figures before submission for DPI, file format, accessibility, panel labels, and readable text.

prompt_templates.title: Create a Basic Figure
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a publication-ready line plot plan for [data description] using matplotlib, with labels, units, colors, and export format.

prompt_templates.title: Adapt to a Journal
prompt_templates.prompt: Adapt my existing figure for [journal], including size, typography, palette, DPI, and file format recommendations.

prompt_templates.title: Design Multi-Panel Layout
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a four-panel figure for [study result], with panel labels, shared styling, error bars, and accessibility checks.

prompt_templates.title: Audit a Figure Workflow
prompt_templates.prompt: Audit this plotting workflow for publication risks, then suggest concrete changes for statistics, accessibility, layout, and export.

output_examples.input: A researcher needs a Nature single-column line plot with 95% confidence intervals.
output_examples.output: A figure plan with Nature width, readable fonts, colorblind colors, vector export, and confidence interval caption guidance.

output_examples.input: A lab has four inconsistent seaborn plots for one manuscript figure.
output: A shared style strategy for all panels.
Export settings for review and submission files.

output_examples.input: A journal rejects a figure because resolution and file format are unsuitable.
output_examples.output: A corrected export checklist covering DPI, vector formats, raster formats, font embedding, and final-size inspection.

best_practices: Choose the target journal and final figure size before building the plot.
Use redundant encodings such as markers or line styles when color carries meaning.
Export vector formats for line art and inspect raster images at final DPI.
anti_patterns: Using red-green palettes, rainbow colormaps, or color alone to encode key comparisons.
Saving scientific plots as JPEG or low-DPI raster images for manuscript submission.
Adding decorative effects, crowded labels, or inconsistent fonts across related panels.

faq.question: Can it create figures from raw data?
faq.answer: It can guide plotting code and styling, but the user must provide clean data and context.

faq.question: Which libraries does it cover?
faq.answer: It covers matplotlib, seaborn, and plotly. The included helper scripts focus on matplotlib.

faq.question: Does it replace journal author instructions?
faq.answer: No. Use it as preparation support, then verify current journal instructions before submission.

faq.question: Can it help with accessibility?
faq.answer: Yes. It emphasizes colorblind-safe palettes, grayscale checks, readable text, and redundant encodings.

faq.question: Does it run statistical analysis?
faq.answer: No. It helps display uncertainty and significance after valid statistical analysis is complete.

faq.question: What output formats can it prepare?
faq.answer: It supports publication workflows for PDF, EPS, SVG, PNG, and TIFF outputs.
